spec_round_protocol.why: Operator: 'one agent produces the spec, the next triggers the agents review until a agent thinks is good to implement. We need to have another gate so agent don't go on forever.' Implemented as successive driver iterations rather than subagents, at the operator's suggestion ('the trigger at 2AM generates the spec and the one at 2:15 reviews it'). A fresh process has no memory of writing the thing it reviews, so the independence is structural rather than merely prompted.
spec_round_protocol.gate: At round 3 without approval, STOP iterating. Ship the artifact as-is, record every unresolved objection in decisions_for_user, and move to the next queue item. Never a fourth round.
how: AUTHOR iteration: write or revise the artifact. Set next_action to 'REVIEW <path> round <K>'. Commit.

REVIEW iteration: read the artifact cold. Do NOT look up who wrote it. Critique against the item's stated review_criteria. Then either (a) set approved=true in the log and set next_action to the implementation step, or (b) write concrete objections and set next_action to 'REVISE <path> round <K+1>'. Commit.
Record the round number in the log entry every time, so the gate is auditable.
spec_round_protocol.research: Web research is authorised and encouraged where it would change the answer. Operator: 'Do any research on the internet that the agents deem necessary. Always think things out before implementing.'

queue.title: Fix the conversation-inheritance tie properly, with a sequence column
queue.why: hub/tests/test_override_inheritance.py::test_the_most_recent_overrides_win fails ~50% in a full chunked run. The test is CORRECT; the code is wrong. A trustworthy suite is a precondition for Q5's audit — a loop culling tests cannot tell a flake from a test it broke.
queue.detail: DO NOT apply the one-line fix proposed in handoff 0050 (adding Conversation.id.desc()). Prep checked it and it does not work: Conversation.id is 'conv-' + short_id(), i.e. random, so id.desc() picks the later-created row only about half the time. It would make the query deterministic-looking while staying arbitrary. The real bug: hub/hub/conversations.py:72 orders by created_at.desc() alone, and two conversations created inside the same clock tick tie — on Windows the default timer granularity is ~15.6ms, so this hits real users, not just tests. Follow the codebase's own precedent: add an autoincrement `sequence` integer primary key to Conversation, exactly as TaskTransition and InboundQueueEntry already do, and read the reasoning already written at hub/hub/db/models.py:695-699. Order by sequence.desc(). Needs a migration in hub/hub/migrations/versions/ that guards for a missing table (see 0033/0034), and CLAUDE.md requires bumping the head assertions in BOTH hub/tests/test_migrations.py and hub/tests/test_project_persistence.py.
queue.verify: Add a regression test that creates two conversations with an identical created_at and asserts the later one wins. Mutation-check it: revert the ordering change and watch that named test fail. Then run the full hub suite three times and confirm test_override_inheritance passes every time.

queue.title: Add a delete-project API and a UI button for it
queue.why: The operator asked for this directly at 02:22, after Q1 discovered no project-delete API exists anywhere in the Hub. Honouring a routine 'remove these test projects' request required stopping the Hub, backing up the database, and sweeping 7,788 rows across 26 tables with hand-written SQL. A product whose only way to remove a project is raw SQL has a real gap, and the operator will hit it again the moment they create the next test project.
queue.detail: Two halves. (1) API: DELETE /api/v1/projects/{project_id} in hub/hub/api/v1/projects.py, with the cascade logic probably belonging in hub/hub/project_lifecycle.py alongside the existing create/open code. DERIVE THE CASCADE FROM EVIDENCE, not from guessing: iteration 1's raw sweep already established which tables carry project-scoped rows — read its log entry and its commit, and reconcile that against hub/hub/db/models.py. Decide explicitly whether to express it as SQLAlchemy cascade='all, delete-orphan' relationships or explicit deletes, and say why. (2) UI: a delete control in the project rail — the 'Configure <project>' affordance already exists (button[data-testid="project-expander-..."] area) — behind a confirmation that requires typing the project name, which is the standard pattern for an irreversible destructive action. Icon component (lucide-react) only; CLAUDE.md forbids a second icon system.
queue.safety: THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT CONSTRAINT: deleting a project must delete HUB ROWS ONLY. It must NEVER touch the workspace directory on disk — that is the operator's actual source code, and an AgentWeave project points at a real working tree. A delete that removes a user's repository is the worst bug this product could ship. Write a test that asserts the workspace directory still exists after a delete, and mutation-check it. Decide separately, and record the choice, whether the .agentweave/project.json binding marker inside that directory should be removed (the binding is gone, so removing it is defensible) or left alone (it lives in the user's directory, so leaving it is the conservative default).
queue.review_criteria: Does the delete touch ONLY database rows, with a test proving the workspace directory survives? Is the cascade derived from the models and iteration 1's evidence rather than guessed, and is anything left orphaned? What happens if the project has a RUNNING run, or an open conversation — refuse, or force, and is that stated? What happens when the operator deletes their LAST project — does the UI handle an empty state or break? Is the confirmation proportionate to an irreversible action? Does it reuse the existing Icon component and rail patterns rather than inventing new ones?
queue.verify: hub/tests/ coverage for: the happy path, the cascade leaving no orphaned rows, the workspace directory surviving (mutation-checked), and the last-project case. Then drive it for real against the live Hub on a THROWAWAY project created for the purpose — never against aw-loop10, which the operator needs intact to answer the 29 parked judgement tasks. If Q4a's harness works, screenshot the confirmation dialog and the resulting empty state.
queue.note: First real user of Q4a's harness, and deliberately so: a confirm dialog and an empty state are simple enough that a screenshot either obviously works or obviously does not. Prove the harness on this before trusting it on Q4's harder visual judgements.

queue.title: Audit every test against the code and cut what does not earn its place
queue.why: Operator: 'Check every test against the code see if they earn their place or if they need to be removed.' Authority granted: delete, on a stated bar, mutation-checked.
queue.detail: Write the bar FIRST, in the log, before deleting anything. Proposed bar — a test may be deleted only if it meets one of: (a) it asserts nothing the code can break (tautological, or asserts only on mocks it set up itself); (b) it duplicates another test's coverage exactly, and deleting it changes no mutation outcome; (c) it tests behaviour that no longer exists. A slow test is NOT grounds for deletion on its own — that is Q2's problem. For every deletion, log the test name, which bar clause it met, and the mutation check that proves the remaining suite still catches the defect the deleted test claimed to catch. Beware the trap already recorded in the autonomous-session skill: a green suite after deleting tests proves nothing by itself.
queue.verify: Per-deletion mutation check. Net test-count and wall-clock before/after. Every deletion reviewable as a diff on the autonomous branch.

queue.title: Explore, then spec: a real desktop app with one global state
queue.why: Operator: 'I also want a full app experience with agentweave no more opening on the browser' and 'agentweave should be global... if I ran agentweave from different folders it creates a different agentweave which is weird. Now that I want it to be a full app opening always restore the same state.'
queue.detail: These are ONE change, not two — a desktop app that opens a different database per launch folder is incoherent, so they must be specified together. Prep already found the root cause of the second half: hub/hub/config.py:9 sets database_url to 'sqlite+aiosqlite:///data/agentweave.db', a RELATIVE path resolved against the Hub process's working directory. Launch from a different folder and you get a different database and therefore a different AgentWeave. Note the multi-project architecture is already correct — src/agentweave/cli.py:828 registers Path.cwd() as a project, which is right; it is the Hub's own state that is wrongly per-folder. Also check src/agentweave/cli.py:176 and :857, which build 'Path.cwd() / hub' and so assume the caller is standing in the AgentWeave repo. Start with an EXPLORATION (openspec/explorations/), not a proposal: the problem is felt but the shape is not settled. Research Tauri, Electron, pywebview, and anything else current, against the existing FastAPI-serving-a-static-bundle architecture; web research is authorised. Weigh: install size, whether it stays pip-installable, code signing, auto-update, OS webview differences, and what a second toolchain costs a zero-runtime-dependency CLI. Then decide where global state should live on each OS. Then a spec round.
queue.review_criteria: Does the exploration actually compare alternatives with evidence rather than assert a winner? Is the global-state location specified per-OS, with a migration path for people who already have a per-folder database they care about? Does it say what happens to an existing data/agentweave.db? Does the desktop shell choice state its rejected alternatives and why?
queue.constraint: NO new language toolchain may be installed this run (no Rust, no Node-for-Electron). Research and specify only; a prototype is allowed only if it needs nothing beyond pip. This is a pre-authorised default, not the operator's stated wish — if the spec concludes a toolchain is required, record that in decisions_for_user rather than installing it.

queue.title: What do popular harnesses have on the UI that AgentWeave lacks
queue.why: Operator: 'After all of that is done if there still time and the loop is not done I want you to work on UI quality of life things.' Explicitly last.
queue.detail: The operator's example: 'When the agent is executing something, file edit, bash, things like that it all show in a work box without much explanation. T3 for example show the details of the things being executed with a different font and a icon which is really nice and give more insight on what's actually happening.' But the scope is deliberately WIDER than that one example — operator: 'that t3 is nice but go beyond compare t3 and other tools. What is nice to have on the UI that we do not have. Is there any functionality in the most popular harnesses that we lack? Investigate everything before implementing.' So: survey real, current tools — read open source where it exists, use the web where it does not. Produce a gap list ranked by what it would give a user, not by how easy it is. Only then propose. Note AgentWeave's Icon component wraps lucide-react and is the ONLY icon system — CLAUDE.md forbids introducing a second one, so any icon work uses it.
queue.review_criteria: Is the survey based on evidence — code read, product used, documentation cited — or on recollection? Is the gap list ranked by user value? Does each proposed item say what it costs to build? Does anything proposed conflict with the single-icon-system rule or the existing theming?
